analysis.one_liner: Requires FDA to certify generic drugs as therapeutically equivalent and bars conflicting state rules.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a single cosponsor or vote, so no change was made to how generic drug approvals are labeled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Food and Drug Administration to state, every time it approves a generic drug, whether that generic is the therapeutic equivalent of the brand-name original — same active ingredients, same dose, same expected clinical effect [S3]. It also would have stopped states from imposing their own, different requirements about therapeutic equivalence, creating one national standard [S2]. The point was to make it easier for pharmacists and health plans to swap cheaper generics for brand-name drugs with confidence [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and anyone who pays for prescriptions — families, employers, and government insurance programs — would benefit from clearer federal certification that a generic works the same as the brand-name drug, supporting faster substitution of cheaper generics [S2]. Generic drug makers would also gain from a uniform national standard instead of a patchwork of state rules [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA to include a finding in each generic drug approval stating whether the drug is the therapeutic equivalent of the brand-name drug — identical active ingredients, dosage form, strength, and expected clinical effect [S3].
Bars states and localities from imposing any requirement on therapeutic equivalence that differs from or adds to the federal standard, so generic makers face one rule instead of fifty [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers would bear the cost: clearer equivalence findings and a uniform national standard make it easier for pharmacies and insurers to substitute cheaper generics, cutting into their sales on drugs that have lost patent protection [S2]. Taxpayers would fund whatever additional FDA review the equivalence findings require.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers losing generic substitution

drawbacks.text: The federal preemption provision would strip states of the power to set stricter or additional therapeutic-equivalence requirements, removing a layer of state-level protection even if the federal standard is adequate [S3].

The FDA already rates generic drugs for therapeutic equivalence in its approved-drug list, so the bill largely codifies existing practice; the added mandate would impose new paperwork and findings with modest incremental benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to patients is real but modest — the bill mostly formalizes a determination FDA already makes, and faster generic substitution saves money. The clearest downside is preemption: states could no longer add their own requirements on therapeutic equivalence, so the national standard would be the only one. Overall a low-stakes, consumer-friendly measure whose cost falls mainly on brand-name drug makers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on October 29, 2003, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S5].
On November 14, 2003, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where no further action was taken before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5].
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor during the entire Congress [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers came out ahead: no equivalence-finding mandate was enacted and no uniform federal standard displaced state rules, so nothing was done to make generic substitution easier. Patients gained nothing because the bill never moved.

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee; it attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on October 29, 2003, and never considered it beyond referral.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on November 14, 2003, and took no action on it for the remaining life of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so there is no record of how the parties stood on it.

industries.note: The bill would have required an FDA equivalence finding with each approval and preempted state requirements, giving generic makers a single national standard and making substitution by pharmacists easier. Their gain comes directly from patients paying less.

Clearer, mandatory equivalence findings and a uniform standard make it easier to swap out brand-name drugs for cheaper generics once patents expire, cutting brand-name sales. Keeping equivalence determinations less prominent serves the brands' interest at patients' expense.
